text: Here I’m going to talk about what you develop in yourself as you reparent your inner child. I’m going to talk about it in terms of three jobs: your loving Nurturer, your safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and your wise Guide. It’s one person doing three jobs rather than getting three more people to move in with you to help with the rent! Each job keeps the others in balance. It’s you that needs to develop these qualities.

Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”
That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!
What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. That might not be how it goes for everyone, and it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help. Do your part for people who are suffering, and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.
Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.
I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.

Science only gets to circle the edges of consciousness, though it finds some wild stuff out there: people functioning with no felt controller, several things cognized at once, split-brain patients who can seem like two knowers sharing a skull, and one recent theory that models minds as nested parallel observers. The full nerdy tour is in the research report. Science gives my argument a third wheel, making it safer to ride, but it will never show nibbāna itself – self and sense organs unweaving into self-presenting light flows of bliss. That requires meditation.

The Parent You Inherited
I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
If it’s a critic, the parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you’re not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one means nothing you do could ever count, and it’s one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” of course your little one doesn’t answer.
But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.
A good routine still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s run in the warden’s tone. Talking back to the warden can feel disloyal, so I’d give that voice a name of its own, like the Critic. Then start a little rap sheet of its lines, with who used to say them and when (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2). Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.
The voice can also pile on. You feel sad, then call yourself pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness. The name-calling is where your Nurturer can step in.

Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people’s first guess is that they didn’t go deep enough. I don’t think that’s it, though, and I don’t think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn’t come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I’d try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations.

A place where people who’ve done the healing first can join without pretending they’re fully finished, and that also has peer practice and enough play that it doesn’t become a permanent repair shop.

The tangle’s heavy by nature (even an arahant feels the first dart), and craving’s what keeps us carrying it. And binding is literally heavy in physics too (quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy). Matter weighs what its binding weighs. Light weighs nothing.

Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, “I can’t imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father.” He doesn’t collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what’s worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest “genuinely tested” him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he’s very proud of both his sons. Then he says, “But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn’t have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective.”

When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! But they get to go for a walk too. Ask your little one what it’s afraid of. I think it just wants to know they’re coming back. Then the Guide can come up with something like “See you in an hour?”

This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it’s about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? Who has to step aside because they’re too close to it? Who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will make sure all the evidence is preserved? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns? What review or appeal is possible without endangering others? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? When is it time to bring in outside help?

“And So That’s the Way It Happened!”
My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. (“Once upon a time…” helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.
Does saying it make the memory fiction? Well, no, it’s still what happened, as far as you remember it, even if some details turn out fuzzy. If the phrase does the trick, leave it at that, no need to narrate the whole thing.
Do keep an ear on who’s narrating, though. If the voice starts sneering, like it’s making fun of the younger you, stop right there (that’s the courtroom creeping back in). Same if you feel more ashamed, or kind of floaty and unreal, since more distance won’t help with that. And when it goes well, it’s a good time to check in with the younger you in that story. What do they need from you now?

Physics backs this up, and I mean literally: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, and roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy. Matter weighs what its binding weighs. This session is now over.
When you come out, remind yourself what day (or date) it is. Look to your left and your right. Look at something near, and something far. Move around a bit, and don’t get up until you feel steady. Make sure you’re actually oriented and alert (the count is supposed to bring you back, but it doesn’t always do the whole job). Take mental note of anything that has come up for you and any actions you need to take regarding it. Then go on and do something normal.

In a large society, the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart. Nobody knows anybody well enough, or for long enough, to tell who can be trusted. Even your next-door neighbor is often a total stranger. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)

And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

Aside from focusing on things in your direct experience, you can also suggest yourself into greater alertness (it's still relaxed-alert, not paranoid-alert). Keep your eyes open. Use a small hand movement each time you make the auto-suggestion that you're gaining increasing clarity. Then stop the hand movement and see where your mind is at. That hand movement is the mental escape into the body's flow. Say something like,
“Starting with your eyes open, press your thumb to your forefinger, gently, and let go. Each time you do, you get a little more awake… Press and let go again, a bit clearer. And once more, and now you’re clearer than when you started. Now stop pressing. In the first second after you stop, is the pressing still echoing somewhere? Start with your fingers, which may still be tingling. Next, see if your breath kept the rhythm going. Then check whether your attention is still waiting for the next press. Or maybe there’s no echo at all. Just notice, sit up straight and work from this level.”

Speak Toward What You Are Building
It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent, just like that Pink Elephant. Being totally independent also isn’t realistic nor ideal, and can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!
But let’s also make sure we don’t hide from shadow stuff with toxic positivity. Grief is natural, and letting tears flow can be immensely therapeutic, as long as they don’t hijack your perspective with a cemented story of what will always be true. If your little one says “he hurt me,” we honestly label that as harm, even if it was also a learning experience. Same for anger, a “No,” who’s responsible, all that. Then once the difficult experience is acknowledged by the Nurturer, the Protector & Guide can lead the way up to more safety and maturity.

Sometimes a session goes great, and a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. Going deeper next time won’t fix that. You just haven’t brought any of it out with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine.

Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship. You’d still belong, just selectively. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.
Day to day, differentiation looks something like this:
- Caring about somebody’s feelings without automatically adopting their opinions or sacrificing your own ground. Their reasons can still change your mind, though.
- Noticing when you agreed in the moment and disagree later: “Wait, why was I nodding along?”
- Noticing when what you thought you knew suddenly feels like water dripping through your hand because of praise or pity, fear or attraction, or something that really resonates with you.
- Disappointing people and withstanding social pressure, and still being recognizably yourself wherever you are (maybe louder in some places). That one can take a while.
- Questioning what you were programmed to believe while holding the discomfort, and without having to stop loving anyone over it.
Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. Sometimes you need to take a break from a family, group or relationship, even if they aren’t doing anything to you. Simply being around them may pull you into that programmed space where listening to what you really want becomes harder. Some people come back later on different terms, and sometimes the break has to be long-term because the pattern of losing yourself with them is deeply entrenched. As you differentiate, you learn to tell which of those apply.
Key developed this identity and differentiation portion of the method, drawing on Murray Bowen’s family-systems work and her own self-therapy.

If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. If you have advice, let them take it in at their own pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.

Five Stages of Reparenting
For now, I think of the whole path in five fairly predictable stages. You might be starting at any point here (and it may change even from hour to hour as well):
1. You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting:
2. Begin to borrow adulthood — remember watching Mr. Rogers or Sesame Street? Those adult role models are what we’re looking for at this stage. This can almost feel like playing house as a kid where you imagined how you’d take care of a baby doll etc.
3. Practice adulting — do at least one part of caring for yourself while support is still there from the previous step.
4. Adult mode itself — after sufficient practice with reparenting, you become a natural at sending love to little you, protecting them, and directing them.
5. Adult and child in relationship — the adult leads. The child isn’t pushed away, but doesn’t have to run the whole life alone. This can actually feel really weird if you’ve been stuck in forced adulthood for a while. Our goal is to go from weird to silly and playful. Lose self-consciousness while gaining self-awareness, if that makes sense!
Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Your little one starts believing the grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore.
Reparenting isn’t an exercise you finish, after all. Say your boss asks you to stay late again. You tell them no and go home feeling okay about it, and nobody had to cry on a meditation cushion for that to happen.

You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue
If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one. Actually, this is one place where the usual inner-child prompt to “ask your little one what they need” can get confusing, because “ask” sounds like you’re supposed to ask a question and then wait for a second voice to answer. Maybe that’s what happens for some people, but you might not be some people (hehe). If talking into an empty room feels silly, small figures on a table can help (so that you feel even more silly!?), like one for your little one and one for the rest of the gang that shows up. Put whichever one’s running the show on a throne. Both ideas come from sections 12.2 and 13.1 of a book called Schema Therapy for Children and Adolescents, which I’ll call ST-CA.
You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and yet still be able to think a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, speak or write them. You might feel more comfortable that way than just staying in imagination land. Then again, maybe what’s actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach. Or perhaps you’re in a place you want to leave. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be nice to do for yourself. And if you don’t know, it’s fine to guess. Maybe it’s some genuine human closeness, or figuring out some way to have more say in your own life.
Life is always switching up on us. You could have a feeling before thoughts, or thoughts might come first and provoke a feeling. They say hindsight is 20/20, but you actually might not even know which happened first.

If You Want to Kill Yourself
Maybe you’re reading this about to act, or with the means close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger. Do the same if you can’t stop yourself, and also when you’re badly disoriented or intoxicated, or can’t tell whether any of this is you. Getting safe first keeps the question of whether life is worth living open long enough to look at.
Then, before getting all philosophical, make sure there’s a real, live grown-up in the room or on the phone, if that’s possible. And as for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who’s doing the noticing (as we discussed in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :). Any part of you that can help keep your body safe, or would rather wait on a decision you can’t undo, is welcome. And if none of them shows up yet? No problem, the questions can wait.

Pattern 10: Meta Model questions — the de-hypnosis tool
To 'Milton Model' is to open things up, so the listener can fill in what fits for them. To 'Meta Model' is to stop and ask, "What do you mean by that?" In order to be ethical with people, you need to do both.
When something sounds true but vague, ask, "What do you mean, specifically?" Then find out according to who, and compared to what. If you hear "always" or "never," check whether it's really every time. If someone's afraid of doing something, ask what exactly would happen if they did. And ask how they know, and what evidence would change their mind.
So when someone is starting to tense up in their body, use the Milton Model to help them soften. And when you feel you're losing track of what's really going on, that's the time for the Meta Model.

Borrow One Competency at a Time
A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
For warmth, think of someone you remember fondly. How would they sit beside your little one? Just make sure it’s someone who liked you the way you were.
For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here. Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you’re about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh!
The Guide can be you too, just a calmer you. That’s a lot easier to imagine than your future healed self. Think back to what (and how) you decided about something like this the last time you were calm. Or ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (like “What would Jesus do?” or “What would Buddha do?”) can give some direction, too, until you develop your own internal compass.

Or if you do get an answer, it could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It’s often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that’s what it wants. If it tells you to do something, I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.

Communes Are Hot Again 🔥
Suddenly, the longing to escape loneliness, which inspired my father’s movie, is everywhere again. Back in 2023, ironically, just the year after Covid lockdowns ended, the U.S. Surgeon General even put out an advisory, saying roughly half of American adults experience loneliness, and it treated social connection as a **public-health** issue.
It’s obvious that a lot of people can’t tolerate modern life in isolation anymore (the UN’s rules for prisoners literally ban more than 15 days of it). Folks may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starving them.
What’s starving them is anomie. We evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows, loves, and trusts everybody. In a large society, the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart, and nobody knows anybody well enough or for long enough to tell who can be trusted—even your next-door neighbor is often a total stranger. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)

The astral plane is a bit different from the 3D. In the astral realm, unconditional love is a true, ultimately powerful physical force. Like a river, or a moat. There’s no evil that can trespass that moat. But don’t assume it will always work like that in the physical plane. It definitely has worked for me sometimes when facing some thugs, but definitely not with others. Loving someone does not mean you leave the front door unlocked with a sign saying “take whatever you want.”
If you’re not able yet (or in the moment) to summon real love for an enemy, you can first send love to your frightened little one from your adult Nurturer. Many people also find they can borrow support from God, Jesus, angels, devas, or whatever loving spiritual presence fits their tradition. If I were to do that, I would still be framing it as “Please help this situation with love” rather than “Strike down the enemy!” But if a presence seems to enjoy your fear, it’s not one of your grown-ups, borrowed or not, whatever it says it is. Same goes if it demands you hurt or use anybody, yourself included.
Borrowing support like that is basically borrowed adulthood. At first you may need to feel protected or loved by something bigger than you, before that love starts to feel like yours, and then bit by bit it starts to become your own. Send some of it down to your frightened little one, and when that’s possible, toward whatever you’re afraid of. Continuing to relate to benevolent spiritual powers/beings is still perfectly fine, but they would surely be happy if they rubbed off on you!
If a voice or urge is directing you towards harm, and you feel at risk of acting on it, as with myself and those ghosts at home, move away from that open window and get some outside support.

One important thing to become aware of when approaching your inner child is your inherited parent script. Your parent script is made up of a collection of rules and ways of treating yourself that you adopted as a child (mostly based on how you were treated by your parent(s)). It doesn’t always take the form of a voice. It is not the inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Guide) that you consciously build. Often this script acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, the script may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.

When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. Say you wake up from a dream soaked in way more feeling and need than anything the session got near. Then this is probably you. A nice session that just wears off is a different thing. I’d ask what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again after your morning coffee. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, dial the practice down by doing it earlier in the day, or for less time.

If the Love Isn’t Coming Yet
If you weren’t loved well as a child, “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn’t close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.
Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It’s scaffolding, and it isn’t a test of whether you were loved enough.
Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).
If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.
Your little one might not take it well at first. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.

My buddy E. told me he had much stronger episodes while driving: for long stretches, his own car and the traffic seemed to disappear. He never had an accident either. God only knows why (luck, a misunderstanding of what was happening, something about how these states work, some mix of those, etc).
Either way, I wouldn’t keep driving through that myself. If you’re having episodes like that, I’d stay away from driving or running machinery until you understand them better. That’s my own CYA showing. 😇

Forgiveness without bypass
We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. However, if we remain in the anger forever, we are allowing the injury to dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. Our boundary with them is crucial to maintain, especially after forgiveness which can tend to weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
You might say to the part of you that got hurt, “I’m not going to use spiritual mumbo jumbo to shush your cries and make you forgive before you're ready. But I’m also not going to build our whole life around this wound forever.”
Forgiving yourself
For self-forgiveness, name what you regret doing, and take responsibility for just that part. Let yourself feel the remorse by taking in the harm done. See how it went against your values. Stop short of making yourself a permanent criminal by identifying with the behaviors you're now abandoning.
Do what you can to put it right. Every so often, come back to how you got to be someone who could do that, until you understand the pattern well enough that it can't drive you anymore.

Once you’ve got your bearings, make your first wish.
"Please show me the next truth. The next symbol or feeling. The question or action that's useful for me at this time, and no more than I can handle."
Stay awake when your mind likes to escape
If your mind keeps drifting off, sit up and open your eyes. Then feel your feet on the floor, and just let your breathing go at its own pace. Tell yourself, "I'm not going anywhere. I'm happily arriving more fully here each moment."
Pick something in the room to look at, and feel your spine at the same time (focusing on two things makes it harder for the mind to use multitasking mode to wander). Then ask yourself what the daydreaming is doing for you. Is it bringing you guidance? Does it help you work through a feeling, or are you using it to avoid something?
Ask for any diffuse benefits to become more practically focused: "If this is guidance, show me what I need to do about it. If I'm avoiding something, bring me gently back to the present and show me what it is."
Make the hypnosis more alert
Aside from focusing on things in your direct experience, you can also suggest yourself into greater alertness (it's still relaxed-alert, not paranoid-alert). Keep your eyes open. Use a small hand movement each time you make the auto-suggestion that you're gaining increasing clarity. Then stop the hand movement and see where your mind is at. That hand movement is the mental escape into the body's flow. Say something like,
“Starting with your eyes open, press your thumb to your forefinger, gently, and let go. As you do, you begin to bring yourself into a place of clearer awareness… Press and let go again, and you’re clearer still. And once more, into the clearest state of awareness yet. Now stop pressing. In the first second after you stop, notice if there’s any echo of the pressing in your fingers, in your breathing, in your attention, or nowhere at all. Just notice, sit up straight and work from this level.”

One more thing about telling whether it helped. A few hours of feeling lighter, with the old feeling back the same day, is a few hours of relief. I’d take that! I just wouldn’t call the problem solved from it, or give the exercise all the credit, especially if you also slept well for once. Jot down what changed and how long it lasted if you want, and then leave it alone.
How many tries is enough? I really don’t know, and I’d be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner (stopping counts). Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too, but if that “nope” sounds like a part of you that’s trying to protect you, I’d hear it out first. If it still says no, that’s your answer. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I’d like to hear about it!
Sometimes a session goes great, and a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. Going deeper next time won’t fix that. You just haven’t brought any of it out with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine.

That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one. I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it all off if things got to be too much. It doesn’t have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I’d listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.

I think most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get away from something painful in themselves, and a lot of it goes back to childhood. That’s spiritual bypassing. Plenty of seekers and gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example. I did it too. It doesn’t mean you’re stupid or crazy.

Borrow Hindsight
I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” It’s a question borrowed from your future self, and I wouldn’t take their answer as gospel. I don’t think a perfect Higher Self is waiting in there with the answers, either (more on that in How This Relates to IFS).
That future you also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they’d just make you some food. If you can’t picture them, make the food yourself, and don’t bother faking a feeling first. A “no” or a pause can count as the food, too.
You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, as long as you don’t assume they’ll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

Not Every Hero Wears A Cape
Set one boundary. “What’s a ‘boundary’?”, I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that’s costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Handle that task you’ve been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! Maybe your little one had grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, and maybe you’ve done it too, so this is how they start to believe you.
You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. “What’s an ‘internal attack’?” Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they’re sarcastic about it, you hear it out instead of snapping back. They don’t trust you yet, and you don’t ask them to. They complain about something, and if they’re right, you say so. All of that shows as clearly to them as the clean room did. It’s evidence you’re safe to be around and that you accept them. Love needs both, but without warmth they can still feel like they’re only being put up with.
Plenty of people are still at the putting-up-with part. Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector’s plain acts and the warmth can come after, which feels backwards, because you’d think you have to feel it first before you could do anything for them. But yeah, bonding starts somewhere. And this is not to say you’ve never done anything to care for yourself. If not, you’d be dead right now. But we’re making additional acts of care intentional now as a base for love to grow.

Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo.

Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving gives way to warmth, or to feeling connected. Some feel held, in the body. Being loved can open grief, too. Someone takes care of you, and you think, “Why does this make me sad?” It can be sadness for the care that was missing. While you’re present and still choosing, stay with it. Once it’s swamping you instead of opening you, slow down (like turning the song off for the night).

So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

If you ever want to retire the shortcut, stop practicing it, take it out of your recordings and any apps that play it, and go back to your usual induction. Decide that while you’re wide awake, and tell yourself so. Don’t be surprised if it still works on you for a while, though, since saying it’s gone doesn’t erase it overnight. You can also keep it, but only to start a session you’ve chosen ahead of time. If it keeps pulling you in when you don’t want it to, or you come out of it disoriented, find someone qualified to help you with it, like a therapist who knows hypnosis.

Maybe you’ve let a small child win at Go Fish and never found a good time to start playing for real. Who wants to be the grown-up who finally wins? Without the Guide, you can slide from looking after your little one into spoiling it the same way. Sweets and screens can pass for loving yourself, and so can getting it out of anything hard. Treats and pampering do better at set times, where they can’t get out of hand. They shouldn’t get canceled as a punishment after a bad day, either (ST-CA, section 17.1.4).

A spiritual opening can come long before there’s much of a Nurturer or Protector around, and it can still be real. What I’d look at afterward is what it did to your love. Has it reached your little one yet? And does anybody notice a difference, like you keeping your word more, or being more patient when someone’s having a hard day?

If nothing comes, that’s fine for now. No need to answer for that part just because you’d set this up as a healing session. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together. It’s forced adulthood, and it sounds like “Nope, all good!” from somebody with a fever who’s cleaning the whole kitchen anyway. Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it. If that’s you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it’s just more of the same. I’d try croaking to someone you trust, “Could you pick up some soup?” If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like “Not now, we’ll go after lunch.”
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it’s okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you’ve texted “hello??” before they’re at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! Blowing up their phone and sulking all night is a different story. Your Guide could help you ask for what you need instead, like a hug before they go and a rough idea of when they’ll be back. Before any of that, though, I’d let your little one say what’s going on. I think it just wants to know they’re coming back.
The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

What I will not use NLP for
Here is a list of things I don't do with NLP, whether I'm hypnotizing myself or someone else:
I don't use NLP to convince anyone an intuition is true. For example, I don't use NLP or hypnosis in general, to do more than initial memory retrieval work. Memories retrieved still need external validation, especially when they were led to (which NLP tends to).
On the other hand, I also don't use NLP to talk anyone out of a real signal. That doesn't mean we can't try to calm unbearable pain, but we must keep access to the awareness of the signal so that we can do the real root cause healing.
For example, I won’t tell anyone to push past their fear before asking what it’s protecting, and I won’t make anyone feel rushed when they want to take time to process the feelings.
I don't use NLP on people without their consent nor to bypass consent via covert commands. Nearly all hypnotists claim that hypnosis cannot violate consent, which is an absurdly ignorant and unethical claim.
That includes not manipulating anyone to feel like their "no" is the ego's resistance we need to overcome, which is another way of saying they are spiritually inferior to me if they disagree with me.
If someone is in an unstable state in which they can't reasonably give consent, I don't use NLP to pretend they did.

The Guide also points beyond itself, toward somewhere you belong that doesn’t ask you to give up being yourself. That might be nature, or existence itself. It might be whatever your tradition sees as ultimate. Love can come from any of these places, and you also belong there, which is a little different. Maybe you’ve felt that outside somewhere, like you didn’t need anybody’s okay to be there. The way in is time in nature and contemplative practice, like meditation.

For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule. And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.

How do you check that? I’d keep what you feel around them in mind, and look at their track record too. Do they respect a no, or keep pushing on it, and what happens when you disagree? If something outside of them backs up what they’re telling you, and it all adds up, that’s a good sign.

Notice the Part That Came Here
Some people hear all this about love and answer, “No. I hate myself.” If that’s what you find, just listen to it, without arguing back. But if you opened this article, something in you wanted things to be different, whatever the rest of you was saying. The same goes if you came to therapy or asked someone for help. Or maybe you’d already decided you were hopeless, and then for some reason you tried again.
What was it? It might have been hope, or desperation. Maybe you were curious, or scared. Some people come here out of duty. Or it was more like, “I’m not going to keep suffering like this.” And maybe it was love. Ask that part what it hoped might happen when it brought you here, and follow that thread.

I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha. The famous stanza I loved is actually from the later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth. The early Pāli texts were already reaching for the same kind of pictures, though. In SN 22.95 form is like foam, feeling is like a bubble, perception is a mirage and consciousness is a magic trick, and Dhammapada 170 tells us to look at the world like a bubble, or a mirage.

Sometimes care isn’t the main thing missing. A meal can help, and so can a boundary, but is that actually targeting the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn’t be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?

Journal With Each Hand
Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand. As titles go, it’s pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings. The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.
And what if all that writing leaves you more confused than when you started? Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all. A memory aid doesn’t have to explain your life. It could be a dated note of what happened, or of what helped. A reminder or a next step works too. Or you can leave yourself a voice note.

Remember those guards from The Urge to Escape, above? Same deal here, so get enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep. Borrowed is fine, as long as it’s from someone steady who won’t try to run your trip for you. But feeling attacked by a demon on a psychedelic is not necessarily paranoia. It can be real, and it’s also not bad unless you’re unprepared. It can be supremely empowering when you can send love and see how it fixes the situation.

To turn this off, stop rehearsing it, take it out of any recordings that you have, stop having it in any apps that are active, and go back to using your regular induction that you have been using. Say that you won’t use it anymore when you are awake, but realize that just saying that it is gone won’t make it go away immediately. If you are finding that you are responding to it when you don’t want to, or you are having problems with being disoriented after using it, get some help from someone who is qualified to help you. If you want to keep it in, you can, but only for the use of starting a session at a later time when you want to. For now, today’s trance will be over when you come out of it.
Make sure to reverse anything you’ve done to alter your state when you come out of it. If you’ve floated, make sure you regain your weight (of your choice, of course). If you’ve shrunk, grow to your normal size again. If you’ve regressed or met parts, make sure you come back to feeling complete in the here and now and acknowledge that your body belongs to you and is under control of the adult mind. If you’ve gone somewhere, make sure you go back the same way. Etcetera. Make sure that the only things you bring out with you are the ones you want to.

If you feel vulnerable, if you feel tightness in your throat, if you feel sadness or fear or like you’re trying to protect something, call upon your Nurturer. If you don’t feel better, or if it continues being hostile towards you, stop trying to deal with it and return to your body and the room.
You don’t have to find out if it’s a guard immediately, and you may not be able to comfort it quickly. Is this way of responding helping you to be clearer and steadier and less hooked?

You Are Worthy of Love. Always.
It’s the same love as back in Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!, the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of … something when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or whatever, was there before you could earn anything. Love from a person is more conditional than that. Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.
Be patient with yourself, and gentle, including with the part of you that thinks you should be over it by now. You are more than your pain and your past. There’s help, and lots of other people are out there learning to look after their own little ones.

Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. If a family, group or relationship won’t let you do this while you’re still part of it, temporary distance may be necessary. And sometimes you need the break anyway, because it’s hard to hear what you actually want while the old programming is still playing in your ear. Some people come back later on different terms. Sometimes the leaving turns out to be permanent, because going back would mean disappearing again. You don’t have to know yet which one yours is. As you differentiate, you learn to tell the difference.

After the day, look at what actually happened. If you did the Protector action(s), not feeling better right away is information to learn from. It doesn’t mean failure. Healing is nonlinear, and sometimes standing up for yourself might make you feel worse at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn’t know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. Hey, we’ve all been there. 🤗

And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

Blaming yourself can be doing a protective job, too. “It’s all my fault” might be your parent’s line, word for word. Then again, if it’s your fault, maybe you can fix it before they leave. I’d stop the cruelty either way. And I’d get curious about what makes it so hard to give up.

Working with your inner child
The two-hand practice
There is a simple and easy body technique to connect with your inner child. Just place one hand in the center of your chest, which physically connects you to your love, and then place your other hand just below that, on your solar plexus, where your inner child can be.
Imagine a divine Love from above, with the inner child below, in the solar plexus area. The inner adult is present. You can also use the hand on the solar plexus to massage that area.
Begin to send love from your heart down to your inner child and just notice what comes up for you. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part's a gift from them, and they don't owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. If you feel resistance, just meet it with love. If you feel or see something, just meet that with love as well. If you can't find any warmth today, just leave your hands where they are and notice what's there. Don't pretend to feel something you don't. Let it go back and forth between your heart and your inner child, like a real conversation.
Keep breathing gently through the whole practice. It works as an induction too: the Sober induction below has it as one of the anchors you can pick.

With that under you, belonging with people can get a lot less desperate. Not all at once, but the Guide keeps watching for the moment your little one starts thinking, “If they stop liking me, I won’t belong anywhere,” and keeps reminding it that a group’s approval isn’t the deepest belonging there is. By the way, this job doesn’t have to be called the Guide. The Wise One works, or your Inner Teacher, and “Guru” does for some people.

You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.

Remember When You Already Did It
My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (If no example comes to mind, try another doorway.)

When I say “unification”, I mean whatever pulls everything together so that a person can talk, cross a road, recognize a friend and answer a text, and it works even when there’s no separate knower in there. Most of my daily life includes that ordinary unification and feels almost like everybody else’s day (well, if they’re happy).

The personal accounts and the way I arrange this practice are my own, especially adaptations like combining body-oriented work and hypnotic work. This combination is not a scientifically validated form of treatment at this time. The Cochrane Collaboration has not yet awarded me their highest medal of honor.
Learning, entering, and returning
Healing the Divided Self, Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick (1995), pp 24-27, 45-50, 83-90, covers a lot of aspects of this post, such as interactive hypnosis, helping the subject learn how to learn by using other senses, learning self hypnosis, making sure the subject comes back at the end, etc. However, this is a professional clinical book, not a self help book, so be careful about trying to use the procedures used with the cases, etc in this book for solo work (and the same goes for its historical claims). Also, Adam Eason and Benjamin Parris's article about self hypnosis for the International Society of Hypnosis should be a useful thing to read (especially the parts that talk about how to learn to learn when you're directing it yourself, and about whether you need another person to help you, and using recordings to help you, etc.)
Indirect language and re-entry cues
For information about using indirect hypnotic language patterns, such as pacing, utilizing, metaphor, and associational cues, etc, see Healing the Divided Self, Phillips and Frederick, 1995, pp 53-57, 96-100, as well as Nimja's tutorial on hypnotic language patterns, and his tutorial on triggers. That's where these techniques come from, but don't blame them for every NLP claim here, or for an example that doesn't suit trauma work (Nimja didn't write or endorse this guide). I adapted the language for my own purposes, and I deliberately used a sequence that would be easy to use for re-entry.

I’d count the milder stuff too, like coming back from trip after trip confused or spaced out. If it gets bad, or it keeps happening when you’re sober, I wouldn’t wait to see a psychiatrist about it. And if you think a medicine you’re on is part of the problem, ask your doctor before you stop. Some, like benzos, can be dangerous to quit all at once. Alcohol too, once your body depends on it.

Hypnosis-specific audit
Before you let a hypnotic recording or a live hypnotist put manipulative suggestions into your skull, interview them a bit:
First, what are they going to do to bring you under? And if you react negatively to something, will they pause to change the script? Make sure they are fine with stopping the whole thing.
And how are they deciding it's working? Just because you seem "out of it" shouldn't be a green light. Are they using sneaky moves to get past your adult judgement, like putting you into identity roles (including age regression)? Walking you down obedience ladders? Your desire for belonging also shouldn't be used for that.
Keep in mind though, you can only answer those last questions by reading the script first. You can't expect them to know what your adult judgement would accept, so make that clear ahead of time.
Will they tell you before they use techniques that affect your memory or behaviors after the session? Like fractionation or cues.
Are they low-key using your body signals to prove their theories? Like oh your hand dropped real fast, so you ARE gay.
And when it's time to come out, will they tell you clearly that the session is over, so you get your normal waking, walking self back? After it's over, check how well your critical thinking is working when you look back on how it went.
If any answer they give you is wishy washy, beware. Ask for the exact script (or the methods used since they probably aren't exactly reading a script). If they don't want to give the secrets away, walk right out that door.

Inner child love
Put your hand over your heart and your other hand on your solar plexus (the two-hand practice in Working with your inner child), and say to yourself in a loving way, “Little one, you are not alone. You don’t have to fix this problem. I’m here now to listen to you.” Make sure you're actually talking to your inner child, not just repeating a script. No warmth today? Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required.
Anxiety script
A script you could use for anxiety is:
Where are my body parts? What are my feet doing? How is my body positioned in the chair? How is my body breathing? How is my body situated in the room?
If you’re there, little one, I’m here. Thank you, guard, for letting me know you’re here. You didn’t have to scream. I got your message.
If there is something we need to do, let me know what the first thing is that we need to do at this moment. If there is nothing to do, help my body stand down. I’m not going to abandon you, but I’m not going to worship you either. I will listen to what you have to say and reality test it and then take some action.

A good routine kept in the warden’s tone still feels like punishment to your little one. If talking back to that voice feels disloyal, give it a name of its own, like the Critic. Write its lines down, with who said them and when. Comfort your little one first, then write a reply to each line, firm or funny but never mean (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2).

People sometimes buy forty acres and then bring all their unprocessed stuff with them to a more scenic location. It’s a more beautiful view for sure, but now you have the conflict PLUS goats. A group that practices together weekly for two years may never own land. So what? It’s already a real piece of community, and it can still make a difference when people are going through a divorce, an illness or grief. Parenting too, and plain old loneliness.

Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

A real-life child of yours, or a calm pet, can also act as a companion that brings out the relationship with your own inner child. My son did that for me, and I think that’s very common for parents. But those are also their own beings with their own needs as well. Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.

The 15-minute daily practice
You don't need to learn a second script for this. It's the same process (gather your attention, notice what's here, respond, wait, and come all the way back), just for fifteen minutes or so. That is long enough to induce yourself (it only takes a few minutes), practice and let it unfold at its own pace, and come out again (that takes a few minutes too). Fifteen minutes is just a handy appointment with yourself, though, and your feelings don't have to keep to it. Five minutes is plenty to see what happens when you simply sit in silence, listening, and you can interrupt yourself at any time to change direction if that feels better.
You can also try other ways of inducing yourself, such as becoming aware of 3 things you can see, 3 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel in your body; then 2 of each, 1 of each. Then count from 5 to 1 and begin to listen. Choose one way to induce yourself. You don't need to try all of them (in fact, stacking them might be counter-productive).
Once you have practiced listening a few times with the recordings, you may want to shorten them to speed up your induction, or even practice without playing them back at all. On the other hand, if you like using the recordings, there is no reason to stop. (Once you know the induction well, the cue from "A shortcut back into hypnosis" can shorten it too.)
As you come out of the process, ask yourself what needed warmth, what needed to be protected, what you need to do differently to be more in accord with truth and love and life. Is there something you want to explore more fully or a capacity you want to build? And most importantly, what can you now carry yourself that you used to have to borrow? If you identified something you needed to do differently, make a plan with yourself to do that thing. The more specific you can be, the more likely you are to change: “If _________ (fill in the cue for the old pattern), then I will do ________ (fill in a small action that will begin to change the pattern).” Then check back later and see how you are doing – sleeping, relating, functioning, etc., not only how impressive the session felt.

First Social Connections, Done Right
Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.
I can’t tell you where to look for people who fit you, but I’d bet on more than one place. Keep the good people you’ve already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if one really fits you. Not every one of them has to click (nobody’s taking attendance). And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support, that’s where I’d want the Protector paying attention.
The same goes for doctors. If a hospital held you against your will, or a treatment hurt you, no wonder asking for help feels scary. Bring someone you trust to speak up for you (it doesn’t have to be the relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment’s for.

The Most Extreme Example
I can tell you one shocking personal story that will make you never trust hypnotists again who maintain that you can’t be manipulated through hypnotism:
My friend P. has a friend named V. V. is a 33rd-degree Free Mason. V. has the ability to get anyone to strip naked and have sex with him within 3 seconds, even via phone call. How is this possible? The only way it could be possible, that I know of, is if people are already hypnotized by mass media/devices with a trigger word that is known by the elites.

Keep the Adult Part of Yourself in Charge
Don’t let a strong state, a charismatic person, a sexual charge, a spiritual claim or any other authority take the place of the adult part of yourself. If it’s legit, it’ll still make sense after you’ve slept on it and asked all your annoying questions, and it can take a no and wait.

In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one burning. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

The closest thing I can compare it to is the out-of-body part of some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and some of those reports (controversially) were verified by others in the room. My room event had nothing like that to check, though, since I wasn’t floating around noticing any details. So those cases can’t back mine up. They just help me show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to go down that rabbit hole, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

And even (or especially) when I am suffering, I try to remember to be grateful for that also, because if not for suffering, I would not even think about how much I have enjoyed not suffering as much, and how much this tribulation will help me to develop more compassion, wisdom, and gratitude in future. It connects me with the plight of the countless other beings suffering at that very moment, authentically bringing up a wellspring of compassion in my heart for all of us. And I see clearly that it is my inner child who is feeling this pain, and what an honor it is that I can be there for him.

How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
What do you picture when you wish someone well? Probably them fed and safe, with people around who like them, stuff like that. Wanting that for somebody is love (babies get this part already), and practical love matters a lot. The horizon of what I can wish for someone is partly shaped by the happiness, peace, and freedom I know are possible.
But maybe you’ve had a big spiritual experience, and for a while you felt a peace or a love you didn’t know existed. After that, “I want you to be happy” can mean something much bigger, almost overnight. That’s why loving-kindness meditation can sound comically simple to someone who’s never been near that, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying “may you be happy” over and over won’t zap you into profound love, but it’s one way people find that love and grow it.
If that bigger happiness makes you curious, I’d follow the curiosity and skip pretending to believe anything. Read people from a few different traditions, say a Sufi poet and a Zen teacher. And if you ever meet someone who’s happy in a way that doesn’t add up, watch how they treat people on a day when everything’s going wrong for them.
Sometimes your little one has enough care, and what’s missing is something else. A hot meal can help, and so can saying no to your boss, but is that actually targeting the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn’t be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?
Curiosity can be enough here, something like “Other people say they’ve felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don’t know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?”

Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. At some point you can ask that part, “What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?” “Tell me what you remember, I’m listening.” works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo!

You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you’ve been staring at the rug. I count that as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it’s in the way. Before you decide where it’s coming from, ask it what it’s trying to stop, or what it wants. You can tell that part something like, “I see you. I’m not going to force my way past you. What’s going on?” Or however you’d actually say that. Then wait and listen patiently.

Sometimes you have a really good session where you feel how much you care about your little one and say what they needed to hear. A few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. For a lot of people, the first thought is that they didn’t go deep enough. I doubt that’s the problem, and the session doesn’t sound like a failure to me. Try a tiny bit of what you did for your little one as you go about your day, because one small thing like that can teach them more than ten more good meditations. Text a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine, for instance. Sending that text can be harder than the meditation was.

What to Make of a Passing Feeling
Here’s where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That’s not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though. If what they did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn’t mean their boundary crossing indicates “They’re evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you’re in your happy place.
Feelings about yourself work the same way. “I feel attracted” or “I feel ashamed” is real as a feeling, but it doesn’t settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche’s pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc. You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don’t have to decide what your pronouns are, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there’s nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see the pattern.
The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later.

While you look, notice what your body does and what feelings or urges show up. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (“You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

After the day, look at what actually happened. Say you did the Protector action(s) and you don’t feel any better, or you feel worse. Standing up for yourself can do that at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess. But did you know how to do it, and why? Were you worn out? Maybe whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. 🤗
